div.p: In a multicore platform, the inter-thread cache interferences can significantly affect the worst-case execution time (WCET) of each real-time task, which is crucial for schedulability analysis. At the same time, the worst-case cache interferences are dependent on how tasks are scheduled to run on different cores, thus creating a circular dependence. In this paper, we present an offline realtime scheduling approach on multicore processors by considering the worst-case inter-thread interferences on shared L2 caches. Our scheduling approach uses a greedy heuristic to generate safe schedules while minimizing the worst-case inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences and WCET. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach can reduce the utilization of the resulting schedule by about 12% on average compared to the cyclic multicore scheduling approaches in our theoretical model.

div.head: I. Introduction
div.p: The rapid development of computing technology and the diminishing return of complex uniprocessors enable the wide use of multicore processors in every computation domain. In particular, real-time systems are expected to benefit from multiprocessors due to the advantages of high performance (throughput), low power consumption and high density.

In multicore processors, the last-level cache such as an L2 cache is often shared by different cores to exploit the aggregate cache space efficiently. This is because a shared L2 cache makes it easier for multiple cooperative threads to share instructions and data, and to reduce the cache synchronization and coherency costs, which become more expensive in separated L2 caches [20]. However, the shared cache memory can lead to possible runtime interferences between tasks running concurrently on different cores. As a result, the performance of each task can be significantly affected, leading to longer worst-case execution time (WCET). For example, it has been shown that L2 cache misses can affect the performance of multicore applications to a much larger extent than L1 cache misses or pipeline hazards [8].

In real-time systems, especially in hard real-time systems, obtaining WCET of a real-time task is essential for schedulability analysis. The worst-case execution time of a task, however, is not only determined by its own attributes, but also affected by architectural factors, such as pipelines, caches or branch predictors. As most research efforts on WCET analysis have been focused on uniprocessors [21], they can not be applied to estimate the WCET for realtime tasks running on multicore processors with shared caches. Moreover, in a multicore processor, the WCET of a task is still dependent on which other tasks are running concurrently on other cores (as they have different intertask cache interferences and thus add different amount of memory latencies to the total execution time), which depends on the schedules generated by the scheduler itself. Therefore, unlike in a uniprocessor where the WCET analysis and scheduling can be generally done independently, a multicore processor with shared caches creates a circular interdependence between WCET analysis and real-time scheduling.

To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first work to study this circular interdependence problem. We propose a heuristic-based strategy to break the interdependence between WCET analysis and scheduling in a multicore environment so that one can schedule real-time tasks on a multicore platform correctly and efficiently. While the proposed approach cannot guarantee optimality, we hope this paper can provide useful insights to the research community towards solving this challenging problem.

In this paper, we focus on studying a dual-core architecture where both cores are symmetric, single-threaded and share a L2 cache. Built on an offline multicore real-time scheduling approach, we propose a heuristic-based method to use the WCET and inter-core cache interference information to safely schedule real-time tasks, while minimizing the worst case inter-thread interferences in the shared L2 cache and the WCET. The experimental results indicate that this enhanced offline scheduling approach can reduce the utilization as compared to a naive multicore scheduling approach that does not consider the interaction between WCET analysis and multicore real-time scheduling.

div.head: II. Background
div.p: Traditionally there are two types of scheduling approaches for the periodic real-time tasks on multiprocessors: global scheduling [14], [7], [1], [19] and partitioning scheduling [4], [18], [16]. While traditional scheduling algorithms work very well for uniprocessors, multicore computing brings a new challenge, which is the interdependence between multicore real-time scheduling and WCET analysis of each concurrent real-time task. Since both traditional partitioning and global scheduling approaches do not consider inter-thread cache interferences on multicore processors, as well as their dependence on the schedules generated, the safety and reliability of these scheduling approaches are questionable for hard real-time and safetycritical systems.

Recently some research efforts have been made to attack real-time scheduling for multicore processors. Anderson et al. studied cache-aware scheduling to discourage coscheduling of the tasks that can worsen the performance of shared caches [3]. A study by the same group showed that it is possible to encourage the tasks from the same multithreaded application sharing a common working set, which will decrease the inter-thread interferences on the shared L2 cache [2]. In [5], a shared-cache-aware approach with more complex heuristics has been proposed, which schedules real-time tasks globally according to various scheduling policies, such as the cache-aware policy and the lost-cause policy. And it demonstrated that this shared-cache-aware approach results in better shared cache performance than global EDF (G-EDF) scheduling approach. While these multicore real-time scheduling approaches generally can be very useful for soft real-time systems, they cannot guarantee safety and reliability for hard real-time systems. An important reason is that the metrics used in those approaches such as working sets are based on either profiling or average-case results, which may be quite different from the worst-case results. Moreover, these approaches do not address the circular interdependence between WCET analysis and multicore real-time scheduling. In contrast, our work is based on accurate multicore WCET and interthread cache interference analysis, and we propose a greedy algorithm to incorporate WCET analysis results into the scheduling to generate correct schedules while minimizing the inter-thread cache misses.

div.head: III. Framework and Assumption
div.p: This paper considers a periodic task model. In a periodic real-time system, a task T can be characterized by the worst-case execution time e(T) and the period p(T), and jobs of T are released successively at the interval of p(T). Hence the deadline of a job J k from T coincides with the release time of job J k+1 , which can be denoted as d(J k ). If a job J k completes its execution after the deadline d (J k ), it will lead to a failure in the hard real-time system, which has strict timing constraints. The utilization of a real-time task u(T) can be defined as e(T) / p(T).

Our Assumption and Limitation: To reduce the complexity and to focus on studying the interplay of multicore WCET analysis and scheduling, this paper makes the following assumptions. First, this paper only considers a simple task model, in which all tasks share a common period and are non-preemptive. For example, a real-time task with complex functions can consist of multiple subtasks. These sub-tasks share the same period of the parent task. Also as these sub-tasks have the same priority with the parent task, they are non-preemptive. Second, this paper only considers the inter-core cache interferences due to instruction accesses. It is important to note that in a multi-core processor, there are also other inter-core interferences such as data interferences, shared bus interferences etc [25]. However, to the best of our knowledge, most state-of-theart multicore timing analysis techniques [22], [23], [24] currently can only analyze instruction interferences. Nevertheless, the problem and approaches studied in this paper are independent of the WCET analysis techniques used. In other words, the proposed methods can also be extended to multicore chips with shared data caches and unified caches as long as their WCET can be accurately analyzed. Third, we assume that there is no job preemption, thus no job would migrate between different cores during its execution in the global scheduling and it is not necessary to take the migration cost into account in our study. Fourth, we focus on studying offline scheduling algorithms for hard real-time systems (all the scheduling decisions are made before the execution of the tasks in the offline scheduling), because online scheduling may not ensure safety and may also incur too much overhead due to the circular dependence of WCET on the scheduling itself.

A framework of the multicore real-time scheduling is proposed here to study and verify the interactions between the multicore real-time scheduling and the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences. It consists of the following components as demonstrated in Figure 1.

Task Management: It is responsible for managing the real-time task sets including reading the binary code of the input tasks and obtaining their period and WCET parameters on a uniprocessor. Also it synchronizes the parameters of computer architecture models among all components, such as the number of cores, cache configurations and so on.

WCET Analyzer: It can not only generate the WCET of a task on a single-core processor, but also conduct the multicore WCET analysis by considering the inter-thread interferences on the shared L2 cache. It provides these fundamental parameters to the Task Management module and the Real-Time Scheduler module.

The multicore WCET analysis method is based on a finegrain approach that uses Extended ILP (Integer Linear Programming) to model all the possible inter-thread cache conflicts [23]. In this approach, a number of ILP equations and inequalities are generated based on the control flow graph and the cache conflict graph of each thread, and the WCET and inter-thread cache interferences can be derived by solving the objective function and ILP equations. More details of this multicore WCET analysis approach can be found at [23].
As our work studies the offline scheduling, the timing cost of the WCET Analyzer is acceptable and will not affect the execution of the generated scheduling as well.

Real-Time Scheduler: It obtains the basic information of the input real-time task set from the Task Management module, and then generates a schedule for the task set on a designated multicore architecture by considering the effect of the inter-thread L2 cache interferences.

Simulation Infrastructure: It simulates the execution of the real-time tasks following the scheduling generated by Real-time Scheduler module. It can simulates various environments such as different number of cores and different cache models. Also it provides performance statistics to verify the validity and performance of the scheduling algorithm.

div.head: IV. Our Approach
div.p: The scheduling algorithms studied in this paper aim at hard real-time systems. In other words, the schedule generated by our multicore scheduling approach must ensure all tasks meet their timing constraints; otherwise, the schedule fails. We propose an approach to generate safe schedules for hard real-time systems, while minimizing the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences by using a greedy scheduling heuristic. Our approach integrates multicore WCET analysis into the offline multicore scheduling, and it can be applied to both partitioning scheduling and global scheduling. Some parameters should be obtained as the prerequisites of our approach, such as the common period of all tasks, the utilization of each task (using the WCET on a single-core processor), the ready time and deadlines of all the jobs of each task.

div.head: A. A Greedy Heuristic to Minimize Inter-thread L2 Cache Interferences
div.p: In principle, it is ideal to find out an optimal schedule that is not only safe, but also leads to the least interthread shared L2 cache interferences. The optimal schedule can minimize the total utilization of the tasks and prevent the L2 cache performance from becoming the bottleneck of the system performance. The problem to find out an optimal schedule can be modeled as a combinatorial optimization problem. Specifically, an optimal combinatorial sequence needs to be derived from multiple independent sequences of various sizes. The computational complexity of this combinatorial optimization problem can be identified as NP-hard. Even though this problem is constrained to a dual-core system in our study, its computational complexity still increases exponentially with the increase of the number of the jobs to be scheduled. Consequently, a suboptimal solution is adopted here by using a greedy heuristic to minimize the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences. The greedy heuristic named Least Inter-thread Interference to Both Cores(LIIBC) is described below. For several ready jobs at a given clock cycle, the following tasks are performed. 1. If both cores are available, two ready jobs are scheduled to both cores respectively at this clock cycle, if the corunning of these jobs leads to the least inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences on both cores among all the ready jobs.

2. If only one core is available, a ready job is scheduled to this core at this clock cycle, if its co-running with the job already scheduled on the other core at the same clock cycle leads to the least inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences on both cores among all the ready jobs.

It should be noted that this greedy heuristic is used only for the simplified periodic task model assumed in this paper, in which each task has the same period. For tasks with different periods or priorities, inter-thread cache interferences can be used as a factor to impact, not to uniquely determine the scheduling priority for achieving the best system utilization, which will be studied in our ongoing work.

div.head: B. Partitioning Scheduling
div.p: In the partitioning scheme, the scheduler begins with task assignment by the heuristic of First-Fit Decreasing Utilization (FFDU) [16]. If the task assignment finishes successfully, the tasks assigned to one core are scheduled by the clock-driven scheduling algorithm [16] first. This core is defined as the first core, hence the other core is defined as the second core. The schedule of the tasks assigned to the second core is generated following the LII P artitioning Scheduling algorithm as described in Algorithm 1.

The inputs of the LII Partitioning Scheduling algorithm are the common period of the tasks on the second core, the ready time and deadline of the jobs of the tasks on the second core, and the schedule of the tasks on the first core. The algorithm begins with defining three variables: the boolean variable success represents the status of the scheduling procedure, which is initialized with true. The boolean variable available denotes the availability of the second core at a given clock cycle before a scheduling decision is made, which is initialized with true. The integer variable clk is defined as the counter of the clock cycle which is assigned as 0 first, and is increased by 1 after each iteration. A priority queue named Ready Job Queue is initialized at line 4. The Ready Job Queue consists of the jobs ready to be scheduled and the priority of each job is determined according to the greedy heuristic of LIIBC. If the ready time of a job equals to the current clock cycle presented by clk, it will be inserted into the Ready Job Queue. If a job existing in the Ready Job Queue is determined to be scheduled at a given clock cycle, it will be removed from the queue.

The main procedure of the algorithm is the following: First, if the ready time of a job equals to current clock cycle denoted by clk, it is added into the Ready Job Queue by the function Add Ready Job at line 6. Second, the function Check Availability at line 8 is used to check the availability of the second core at the current clock cycle, which checks if the execution of any scheduled job in Second Core Schedule occupies the current clock cycle. If the second core is not available at current clock cycle, the algorithm continues to the scheduling procedure for the next clock cycle and increases clk by 1 at line 19.

Otherwise, a job already scheduled on the first core is identified by the function F ind Scheduled Job at line 10. This job occupies the first core at the current clock cycle and it is defined as Job 1. To schedule a job at the current clock cycle on the second core, the function F ind LII Job at line 11 is implemented via several steps: First, the worstcase inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences between Job 1 and each job in Ready Job Queue are calculated by calling the WCET analyzer described in Section III. Then all the ready jobs are sorted in the increasing order of their worst-case inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences with Job 1. Finally, the job having the least worst-case interthread shared L2 cache interferences with Job 1 is assigned the highest priority and is scheduled at the current clock cycle according the greedy heuristic of LIIBC. This job is defined as Job 2. The function Job Deadline Check checks if both Job 1 and Job 2 can meet their respective deadline by calculating their finish time, which is the sum of their starting time and their WCET by considering the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences. Noted that although the scheduling decision for Job 1 has been made on the first core, its WCET is changed due to the interthread shared L2 cache interferences if it is co-running with Job 2, so Job 1 still needs to be examined. If either Job 1 or Job 2 misses its deadline, the scheduling procedure fails and success is assigned with false. Otherwise, Job 2 is added into Second Core Schedule with the starting time of clk by the function Add Scheduled Job at line 14, also it is removed from Ready Job Queue by the function Remove Ready Job at line 15.

The scheduling procedure is repeated for each clock cycle by increasing clk by 1 for each iteration. The algorithm is terminated if the scheduling procedure fails or if clk reaches the common period. If the algorithm ends in case that success is true, Second Core Schedule is returned as the output.

div.head: C. Global Scheduling
div.p: In the global scheme, a global schedule is generated for both cores following the LII Global Scheduling algorithm as described in Algorithm 2. We define one core as the first core, and the other as the second core. The inputs of the LII Global Scheduling algorithm are similar with those of the LII P artitioning Scheduling algorithm, except that the ready time and deadline of the jobs and the common period should be derived from all the tasks in the system. The LII Global Scheduling algorithm also begins with defining some variables and initializing the data structure of Ready Job Queue. Noted that the variable available is an integer here, which indicates the availability of both cores: 2 means both cores are available; 0 repre- 25: end sents only the first core is free; 1 represents only the second core is free; and -1 denotes that no core is available.

The scheduling procedure begins with adding the jobs into the Ready Job Queue if the ready time of the jobs equals to the current clock cycle by using the function Add Ready Job at line 7. And the availability of both cores at the current clock cycle is checked by examining all the scheduled jobs already in Global Schedule in the function Check Availability at line 8. There are several different situations according to the availability of both cores at the current clock cycle: If both cores are available, the function F ind LII P air finds a pair of jobs with the least inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences following the greedy heuristic of LIIBC at line 10. This function calls the WCET analyzer to calculate the worstcase inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences between any pair of jobs in Ready Job Queue, and sorts these pairs of jobs in the increasing order of the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences. The pair with the least inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences is returned as Job P air. Then the deadlines of both jobs in the pair are checked with their WCETs including the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences in the function Job Deadline Check at line 11. If both jobs pass the deadline checking, they are added into Global Schedule (either job can be scheduled to either core) at line 13, and they are removed from Ready Job Queue at line 14. Otherwise, success is returned as false to indicate that the scheduling procedure fails.

div.head: D. Computational Complexity
div.p: The computational complexity of both scheduling algorithms depends on the number of scheduling decisions and the complexity to find the scheduling jobs with the least worst-case inter-thread cache interferences according to the greedy heuristic of LIIBC. Assuming that N jobs need to be scheduled, the number of scheduling decisions is N . In the partitioning scheme, the complexity to find a ready job with the least inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences is O(N logN ) by using the quick sort algorithm. Therefore the computational complexity of the partitioning scheduling of our approach is O(N 2 logN ). For the global scheme, as the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences are computed between any pair of ready jobs if both cores are available, there are N 2 pairs of jobs to be handled. So the complexity to find the qualified pair of ready jobs is O(2N 2 logN ) by using the quick sort algorithm. Therefore, the computational complexity of the global scheduling of our approach is O(2N 3 logN ).

div.head: V. Evaluation Methodology
div.p: Our multicore scheduling framework is implemented and evaluated on top of a multicore simulator by extending Sim-pleScalar [10]. The WCET analyzer consists of a front end and a back end. The front end of the WCET analyzer compiles both task benchmarks into COFF format binary code by gcc compiler, which is targeted to SimpleScalar. Then it obtains the global Control Flow Graph(CFG) and related information of the instructions by disassembling the binary code generated above. Subsequently the back end compiler performs static cache analysis [9] with the enhanced Extended ILP method [23]. A commercial ILP solver-CPLEX [11] is used to solve the ILP problem to obtain the estimated WCET. The basic configuration of the simulated dual-core processor is shown in Table I.

In our experiments, we select fourteen benchmarks from Mälardalen WCET benchmark suite [17] as the real-time tasks to be scheduled, whose estimated and simulated worst-case performance on a single core are demonstrated in Table II.

We design 45 task sets consisting of the tasks which are randomly selected from the fourteen real-time benchmark. The number of tasks in a task set ranges from 4 to 14 to achieve various complexity of the scheduling. In our experiments, these task set instances are scheduled by four different approaches as listed below: P Base Scheme: the basic partitioning scheduling approach that first assigns the tasks to each core with the heuristic of FFDU [16], then the tasks on each core are scheduled by the cyclic scheduling method respectively without considering the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences. However, the latencies caused by the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences are added to the resulting schedule to reflect the actual WCET at runtime. G Base Scheme: the basic global scheduling approach that schedules all the tasks to both cores with a global ready job queue by the cyclic scheduling method, which does not consider the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences. However, the latencies caused by the inter-thread L2 cache interferences are added to the resulting schedule to reflect the actual WCET at runtime. P LII Scheme: the partitioning scheduling approach following the algorithm LII P artitioning Scheduling to minimize the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences as described in Section IV-B.
G LII Scheme: the global scheduling approach following the algorithm LII Global Scheduling to minimize the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences as described in Section IV-C.

div.head: VI. Experimental Results
div.p: First, we randomly select 8 task sets to be scheduled by all four scheduling schemes , and the number of the tasks in these task sets ranges from 4 to 12 and their common periods vary between 50000 and 180000 cycles as shown in Table III. Figure 2 shows the normalized worst-case utilization, L2 cache miss rate and inter-thread shared L2 cache misses of P LII scheme and G LII scheme, which are normalized to those of the P Base scheme and G Base scheme, respectively. we can see, the utilization, the L2 cache miss rate, and the inter-thread shared L2 cache misses of all these 8 experiments are lower in the P LII scheme and the G LII scheme as compared to the P Base scheme and G Base scheme respectively. For example, in task set 1, the worst-case utilization, the L2 cache miss rate, and the number of inter-thread shared L2 cache misses in the P LII scheme are 12.84%, 9.7%, and 22.55% lower than those of the P Base scheme respectively. Similarly, the worst-case utilization, the L2 cache miss rate, and the number of inter-thread shared L2 cache misses in G LII scheme are 15.28%, 11.67%, and 28.11% lower than those of the G Base scheme respectively. The main reason for these results is the following. As the utilization of a task is determined by its execution cost and period, and its execution cost is supposed to be fixed without considering the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences, the number of inter-thread shared L2 cache misses that varies with different schedules can become an important factor to determine the total utilization of a schedule for a task set running on a multicore processor. In other words, less inter-thread shared L2 cache misses can result in lower execution cost The benchmarks and periods of the experimental task sets.

of the jobs scheduled, hence decreasing the total utilization of the schedule for a task set. Also the reduction of the inter-thread shared L2 cache misses may decrease the L2 cache miss rate of the jobs scheduled.

It is well known that the schedulability of a task set can be determined by comparing its total utilization with the system utilization. In principle, if the total utilization of a task set does not exceed the utilization of a system, it is supposed to be able to be scheduled on this system [16]. In other words, a schedule for a task set with lower utilization is more likely to be scheduled successfully on a system than other schedules of this task set that result in higher utilization. Therefore, the schedules generated by our approaches (i.e. P LII and G LII) have better schedulability than those generated by the basic schemes (i.e. P Base and G Base).

In order to illustrate the generality of our approach, we also applied these four scheduling schemes to the other 37 task sets (besides the 8 task sets listed in Table III). Figure 3 shows the estimated worst-case results that are averaged across all these task sets. We observe that the average utilization of the scheduling results of the P LII scheme are about 11.38% lower than that of the P Base scheme, while G LII can reduce the utilization by about 10.46% on average as compared to the G Base scheme. Also the averaged L2 cache miss rate of P LII scheme is about 9.39% lower than that of the P Base scheme, and the averaged L2 cache miss rate of the G LII scheme is about 11.71% lower than that of the G Base scheme. All these results confirm the advantages of the P LII scheme and the G LII scheme. Figure 4 gives the simulated worst-case results that are averaged across all these 45 task sets, in which we observe the superiority of the P LII scheme and the G LII scheme over the P Base scheme and the G Base scheme respectively.

div.head: VII. Concluding Remarks
div.p: Since the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences can make the WCET of a real-time thread vary significantly on multicore processors, they can have profound influence on the scheduling of the multicore real-time systems. Consequently, it is important to investigate the interaction between the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences and the multicore real-time scheduling to safely and ef-ficiently schedule real-time tasks on multicore processors with shared L2 caches. As the first work to attack this important and new problem, this paper focuses on studying a heuristic-based offline scheduling approach that aims at minimizing the inter-thread shared L2 cache interferences while scheduling real-time tasks on multicore processors.

Our experimental results indicate that our approach can lower the utilization of the generated schedule by decreasing the L2 cache miss rate both in the partitioning scheme and the global scheme. Therefore they are likely to generate successful schedules with stricter timing constraints for the task model studied. Also, it is possible to reduce the Fig. 3. In this work, we assume a limited model, i.e., all the tasks share a common period to develop the proof-of-concept study for the challenging interactions between multicore scheduling and inter-thread shared cache interferences. In our future work, we would like to extend our work to tasks with different periods and priorities. Also, we plan to evaluate the scalability of our approach on processors with more cores such as 4 cores and 8 cores.
